# Downtime

The pressure's off. That’s not the same as being finished — you're in the middle of something, and this is where you get ready for the next part of it.

Think of downtime as Reset at a larger scale. It does two things: puts you back together, and gets you ready to go again. It isn’t a pause — the city keeps churning while you rest, and so does everyone in it: allies, enemies, and those in between. It’s also not a mode you switch into — the term represents the crew simply taking a break from things for a while.

> **CALLOUT: Three Speeds**
>
> Time moves differently depending on what's happening. Ordinary play runs about even — a conversation takes about as long as a conversation. An encounter slows down hard: three to five seconds a turn, and an hour at the table might cover ten minutes of the city's evening. Downtime does the opposite. An hour of play can cover a week, and nobody narrates the week.
>
> So don't account for it hour by hour. Nobody needs to hear that you read for a while, then saw to the armor, then sat down with the gun. Say what you're working on, what you're spending to get it done, and roll when something's genuinely uncertain. The GM fills in the rest.

Downtime is usually your call — the crew pulls back, regroups, and works out what happens next. What you don't decide is how much you get. The city has its own schedule, and if something is already moving toward you, the week you planned on becomes four hours and a message you'd rather not have gotten. You can ignore the message. What you can't do is make it wait until you’re ready.

One session might not touch downtime at all; the next can pass entirely as roleplay without an encounter in sight — a night of shopping the Goblin Market, arguing strategy, and working out where the crew goes next. That's as much a session as a standoff, an escape, or wall-to-wall violence. Across months of play, it's where most of what your character becomes actually happens.

## What Comes Back

**Health.** Health returns naturally on its own or through focused medical care and attention.

- **Natural Healing:** With food, shelter, and real rest, you recover HP equal to your BOD each day. A BOD 5 character rebuilds a Health Level a day; five hard days puts the whole ladder back. Push on instead of resting and the GM may halve that.

- **Focused Healing:** Med kits, chems, nanites, or legitimate professional care in a clinic or hospital. Healing rate here is based on the type of care you receive, but it’s always faster than Natural Healing. The *Injured* Condition must be resolved through Focused Healing.

**Exhaustion.** Cyborgs and Arcanists run on Tolerance (TOL) and Exhaustion. Once they’re Exhausted they can’t do much else. The recovery rate here is an hour of rest or meditation per point, uninterrupted. Interrupted means the hour didn't count, not that it half-counted. More information on Exhaustion is found in these Archetypes.

**Sanity.** Like Exhaustion, SAN comes back with time and effort. Meditation and VR therapy are the most common methods, but you and your GM can work out what works for you. The base recovery rate is 5% SAN recovered per hour of uninterrupted rest or meditation. VR therapy doubles that recovery rate.

**Gear.** Armor Integrity comes back through repair kits and shops. Ammunition and consumables come back by buying more of them.

## What Doesn't

**Luck.** Luck refreshes when a session ends, not when your character sleeps. A week of downtime inside a single session buys you nothing.

**Withering damage.** Wounds from silver, UV, and the rest of what's built to unmake the supernatural close at the ordinary human rate, whatever you are. Regeneration doesn't touch them, but medicine and rest still do.

**Massive damage.** When high powered explosives remove your limbs, you’ve got to spend some Çredits or favors to get a version of them back.

**What you spent.** Çredits are gone. Favors are called. The contact you burned to get the meeting is still burned.

**Your name.** Reputation doesn't rest either, and neither does anybody who's already decided how they feel about you.

> **CALLOUT: Working Hurt**
>
> Nothing stops you pushing on at half health. The work is there, the money is needed, and the clinic can wait. Plenty of operators in this city have made that call, and most of them have made it more than once.
>
> What it costs is margin. Pain follows you into the next encounter. The Health Levels you didn't get back aren't there when something goes wrong. The armor you didn't repair fails at the moment it was supposed to matter.
>
> Nothing dramatic happens the first time. It happens the third time.

## Getting Ready

Most of downtime isn't mechanical. Everybody's got somewhere — a lock on the door, a clean shirt in the drawer, and a place to sleep. Yours might be an apartment, a cot against the wall of the garage, or somewhere the daylight can't reach. That's where this happens: one of you running searches, one of you cleaning a weapon, something simmering that won't be ready for six hours. It's all at once, and none of it needs turn order. Somewhere in all that, the crew works out what they're actually doing.

- **Work the problem.** Ask around, call in what you're owed, find out who owns the building before you're standing in it — and, eventually, who owns them. Investigation and Streetwise do more across three days than they ever do across three seconds. The immediate question gets answered in an afternoon. The one you've been circling since the beginning takes months, and it gets assembled here or not at all.

- **Prepare what needs preparing.** Rituals take the time they take and can't be hurried. Gear gets modified, ammunition gets bought, and somebody sees to whatever the last few days did to the vehicle.

- **Decide.** Where you're pushing next, what you're willing to spend to get there, and who in the crew isn't happy about the answer.

- **Take work, if you need work.** CRANK is there when the money runs short, and a job on the board is sometimes the fastest way to get near something you couldn't reach otherwise.

**Show the work.** IP spent between sessions has to land somewhere in the fiction. New skill ranks, a Milestone, a spell that wasn't in your book last month — all of it came from somewhere. Somebody taught you. You practiced until it took. Whatever nearly killed you last week changed what you're capable of. Nobody wakes up three points better with a gun; downtime is where the character spends hours at the firing range and catches up to the sheet.

The most important things in this game rarely happen during an encounter. They happen in the quiet part, when somebody finally says the thing they've been holding since the warehouse.

## While You're Resting

The city keeps its hours. Somebody filed the repair on the door you forced. Somebody reviewed the gap in the footage. The contact you left running down leads finally has a name. A faction that was three moves away from something is now two moves away, and none of it waited for you to be ready.

Downtime is when consequences arrive, because it's the first time you've been still long enough for them to reach you. Consequences aren't punishment — they're what your choices produced. Some of it helps. Some of it doesn't. Most of it takes a while to tell which.

All of this is why downtime rarely gets the last word. Expect the GM to find a reason for something to happen before you're finished resting — a knock at the door, a haptic buzz on your SMARTbrace, or a debt settled without being asked. That reason is usually the next session, and it's already moving by the time you hear about it.

Then the crew decides it's time, which is not the same as being ready.
